source.title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
source.authors: Runjin Chen; Andy Arditi; Henry Sleight; Owain Evans; J. Lindsey

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses SAE decomposition and causal feature steering in LLMs, a different method from the original toy-network work, and reports results relevant to whether SAE-recoverable features occur in LLM representations.
record.gate_note: Appendix M reports SAE features aligned with persona vectors and their trait-expression scores when steered; those results are included. Results on persona-vector steering, finetuning, monitoring, and data filtering are not rows because they do not measure the claim's superposition geometry or SAE feature recovery. Results cited from other work are also excluded.
record.test_reason: The SAE work (Appendix M) uses BatchTopK SAEs as a tool to break persona vectors into interpretable features. It does not test whether sparse features exist or are recoverable in Qwen. No reconstruction error, sparsity or dead-feature statistics, monosemanticity measure, or comparison with neuron or random bases is reported. Features are interpreted by auto-interpretability. The steering scores in Tables 8–10 are the top 5 of the 50 most-aligned features, sorted by the score itself, with no baseline. The rest of the paper (persona-vector extraction, steering, monitoring, data filtering) does not address superposition.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right for Appendix M, but the paper's main conclusion is different. An automated pipeline extracts persona vectors (difference-in-means directions) that can monitor and steer trait shifts, mitigate or prevent finetuning-induced shifts, and flag training data. The SAE decomposition is labelled an initial exploration.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies LLM persona vectors and decomposes them using BatchTopK SAEs, then steers with selected SAE decoder directions. It does not use the original toy-network superposition setup or test its geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SAE-feature results are at layer 20 for evil and sycophancy and layer 16 for hallucination; steering coefficients also differ by trait. The SAEs were trained at varying sparsities, while the analysis focuses on k = 64.

fits_no_version.finding: Decoder directions of SAE features most cosine-aligned with a persona vector (cosine about 0.2–0.44) can each steer Qwen2.5-7B toward the trait. The reported top-5 features reach TES about 79–99.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Coarse contrastive concept directions in LLMs decompose into several finer SAE features, each causally sufficient to elicit the behaviour.

record.problems: For the claim-relevant SAE analysis, only one model is examined; the authors call it an initial exploration. The reported feature scores have no stated uncertainty or explicit baseline in Tables 8–10. The paper does not test whether the features are complete, stable, canonical, or distributed across neurons.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant rows omitted. The remaining top-50 feature analyses and qualitative examples in Appendix M are not separately scored results in the supplied text.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity sweep, or geometry.
All: no analysis of causes of polysemanticity.
Spread of features across neurons; SAE recovery quality (reconstruction, sparsity, interpretability rates versus baselines). Only an anecdotal SAE decomposition is given.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The SAE results are qualitative and selection-based: the reported TES values are the maximum of a ranked list, with no control steering. They show the authors' tool works, not that superposition or SAE recovery holds.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, sparse-feature capacity sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry are tested.
No test of neuron polysemanticity as competition for limited capacity or of dedicated dimensions for important features.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity evidences superposition.
The study examines SAE-recoverable features in Qwen persona vectors, but does not measure feature spread across neurons or establish prevalence across LLMs.
No test of SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonical status.
The study analyzes vector directions and SAE decoder features but does not compare one-dimensional with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.operation_detail: Steered with the decoder direction of SAE feature 12061.
rows.measure: Trait expression score after feature steering (TES); feature/persona-vector cosine similarity also reported.
rows.note: The feature is described as detecting insulting, abusive, and derogatory language.
rows.check: Selection value: top-5 of 50 features ranked by the same TES score that is reported. No baseline (random or unaligned feature) is given, and the measure is trait expression, not feature recovery or superposition.

reader_labels.condition: Qwen-2.5-7B-Chat SAE feature steering, evil and sycophancy at layer 20 and hallucination at layer 16
reader_labels.reason: The paper identifies interpretable SAE decoder features aligned with persona vectors and reports that steering individual feature directions produces the associated trait-expression scores (M8-Evil-12061 through M8-Hallucination-2220).
